content: The sterile male mosquitoes are released into the environment, typically within a period of fewer than 10 days. Surveillance efforts are conducted only during the active release phase and continue as long as sterile insect technique (SIT) mosquitoes are detected in the release area. Active participation from local citizens is crucial for the success of these programs, and it is recommended that relevant authorities promote public involvement to ensure sustained success in the field. Sentinel sites can be established and monitored to evaluate the impact of the SIT program on disease incidence and prevalence. These sites provide critical data for assessing the effectiveness of the intervention. In terms of regulatory pathways, the process of obtaining permits and authorizations for SIT mosquito releases varies across countries. Typically, the national authority responsible for such approvals falls under one of three ministries: agriculture, environment, or health. In some cases, specialized agencies are consulted for their expertise and recommendations to the certifying authority. Local authorities, representing the government in specific geographic areas, also play a role in the approval process. In Montenegro, the importation of irradiated sterile Aedes albopictus mosquitoes required authorization from the Directorate for Environment, which operates under the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Tourism. Expert input was provided by the Agency for Nature and Environment Protection (EPA Montenegro) and the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development. It was noted that there was no prior authorization for the importation of Aedes albopictus under the law on nature protection. This species is neither listed as a protected species nor as a non-protected wild animal, plant, or fungus that can be used for commercial purposes. The Ministry of Agriculture clarified that no permit was required for the release of sterile mosquitoes in the specified area, as the mosquitoes were reared from eggs collected locally in Montenegro, eliminating the risk of introducing new genomes. In Germany, the release of sterile Aedes albopictus mosquitoes required a permit from local authorities. The permit specified the release location, mosquito density per hectare, and the designated scientific leader. Additional requirements included ensuring no adverse impact on the existing ecosystem, demonstrating the effectiveness of reducing invasive species, and confirming no risks associated with the release, as male mosquitoes do not bite. A report summarizing the outcomes of the experiment was required to be submitted to the regulatory body upon completion. In France, local production of sterile mosquitoes began in 2009 on the island of La Réunion. However, field release permits were not granted until 2017, as the project was considered to be in Phase I development. Following consultations between various ministries and the High Council for Biotechnology (HCB), a formal request for sterile insect release was resubmitted. The ministries of health and environment sought expert input from the High Council for Public Health (HCSP) and the French Biodiversity Agency (AFB) on risk assessments for workers and the local population, public acceptance procedures, and precautionary measures for supervising releases. In 2018, the Prefecture of La Réunion authorized the release of irradiated sterile males under Phase II testing regulations. The HCSP emphasized the importance of presenting public health programs in an accessible manner to ensure community acceptance, even if direct participation is not required. In Italy, pilot tests of SIT against Aedes albopictus were conducted between 2004 and 2009, yielding promising results. No specific authorization was required for these field trials. These examples highlight the variability in regulatory requirements across countries, with no universal rule emerging from the different field trials. The success of SIT programs depends on the mass production of high-quality sterile male mosquitoes in dedicated facilities. The technological framework for mass rearing, sterilization, release, and quality control of sterile Aedes mosquitoes has been developed, with standard operating procedures and guidelines available. However, regulatory oversight and risk assessments for health and environmental impacts vary significantly between countries. A global approach to standardizing these processes is necessary to ensure the effective deployment of this technology.
